notes: A CAPITAL ALLOWANCE SCHEDULE, OFF UNLESS YOU TURN IT ON. If you do nothing, nothing changes: no new menu entry, no new question on the asset form, and no figure computed differently anywhere. WHO IT IS FOR. Capital allowances belong to a corporate income tax return. Under the Third Schedule to the Income Tax Act, 2015 (Act 896) they replace accounting depreciation for tax purposes, so a business that files no such return has no use for them — which is why this stays out of the way until you say otherwise, at Settings, Tax, Capital Allowances. WHAT IT PRODUCES. A workpaper, not a return. For the year you choose it shows, for each class: opening written-down value, additions, disposals, the allowance and the closing written-down value — with the assets behind each class listed underneath, and an Excel export of the whole thing. It stops there. It does NOT compute chargeable income and it does NOT compute tax. Those are your accountant’s to make from this schedule, and a figure presented here as “the tax” would be an assessment. WHY THIS IS NOT YOUR DEPRECIATION. Classes 1 to 3 are POOLED: the whole class carries one balance and an asset’s own written-down value is never tracked at all. An addition raises the pool by cost, a disposal lowers it by the MONEY RECEIVED rather than by book value, and the allowance is the rate applied to what is left — 40 per cent for computers and data-handling equipment, 30 per cent for vehicles, plant and machinery, 20 per cent for furniture, fixtures, vessels and anything not in another class. Buildings and structures are different again: 10 per cent of COST every year, straight line, per asset. And when disposals come to more than the pool holds, the excess is a BALANCING CHARGE — income to be taxed, not a deduction. The schedule shows it in its own column and never nets it into the allowance, because netting would understate the tax twice over. NOTHING IS GUESSED. An asset with no capital allowance class is NAMED on the schedule and put in no pool. The category on the asset record is a description, not a tax classification, and the app will not read one as the other: a pickup and a filing cabinet fall in different classes at different rates, and that judgement is yours. The same is true of an asset with no purchase date, and of a written-down value you bring forward for a pool — if your register also holds assets from before that year, the schedule says so rather than quietly counting them twice. ONE NEW COLUMN AND ONE NEW TABLE; no existing data changes. This installs straight over the previous version. Please still take a backup first: Backup & Export, Back up now.
